lessons.title: Pledged Shares: Reading the Early Warning on screener.in

body.text: A pledge turns the promoter's shares into a lender's collateral. If the price falls far enough, the lender decides when those shares hit the market, not the promoter.

children.text: In the last lesson you learned to read how much of a company the promoter owns. This lesson asks a sharper question: how much of that stake does the promoter actually control? When promoters pledge shares to raise a loan, usually from a bank or NBFC, those shares stay in their name but are locked as security. A promoter holding 55% with 80% of it pledged is in a very different position from one holding 55% with nothing pledged, even though both look identical in the headline shareholding number.

markDefs.definition: Loan amount divided by the current market value of the pledged shares. As the share price falls, LTV rises even though the loan has not changed.
When a lender enforces its right over pledged shares, transfers them to itself, and usually sells them in the market to recover the loan.

body.latex: \text{LTV} = \frac{\text{Loan Outstanding}}{\text{Pledged Shares} \times \text{Share Price}} \qquad \text{Trigger Price} = \text{Current Price} \times \frac{\text{Current LTV}}{\text{Trigger LTV}}
body.caption: The loan stays fixed, so LTV moves inversely with the share price

children.text: Worked Example: How Close Is the Trigger?

A promoter pledges 2 crore shares when the stock trades at ₹500, so the collateral is worth ₹1,000 crore. The lender advances ₹500 crore, a 50% LTV. The agreement says a margin call is triggered at 60% LTV and invocation at 80% LTV.

body.caption: Pledge triggers for a ₹500 crore loan against 2 crore shares

body.title: Share price vs pledge trigger levels (illustrative)

children.text: Look at month 7 and month 8. Once the price crosses ₹312.50, the lender sells pledged shares into a market that is already falling. That selling pushes the price lower, which pushes LTV on the promoter's other pledges higher, which triggers more selling. The stock did not fall to ₹240 because the business got 52% worse in eight months. It fell because forced sellers do not care about valuation.

body.title: Find the Invocation Price
body.prompt: A stock trades at ₹400. The promoter's pledge loan is currently at 50% LTV, and the loan agreement allows the lender to invoke the pledge at 75% LTV. Assuming no top-up and no change in the loan amount, at what share price does invocation get triggered?
body.explanation: Trigger price = ₹400 × (50% ÷ 75%) = ₹400 × 0.6667 = ₹266.67. That is a fall of one third, about 33.3%, from the current price. Any stock that can fall a third in a bad market is only one bad market away from forced selling.

children.text: Reading the Number: Two Ways Pledges Are Expressed

Screener.in reports pledged shares as 'Pledged percentage', which is the share of the promoter's holding that is pledged. You can add it to the key ratios on a company page or use it as a filter in a screen, for example Pledged percentage greater than 20. The BSE shareholding pattern shows the same data as a share count and as a percentage of total shares. Both are useful, but they answer different questions.

body.latex: \text{Pledged as \% of Total Shares} = \text{Promoter Holding \%} \times \text{Pledged \% of Promoter Holding}
body.caption: Converting screener.in's pledged percentage into the share of the whole company at risk of forced selling

body.title: Which Pledge Number Answers Which Question

columns.label: % of Promoter Holding
points: The figure screener.in shows as Pledged percentage
Tells you how financially stretched the promoter is
Tells you how much control is at risk if lenders sell
Above 50% means the promoter's control depends on the lenders

columns.label: % of Total Shares
points: Shown in the detailed shareholding pattern on BSE and NSE
Tells you how much supply could hit the market in forced selling
Compare it with average daily traded volume to gauge price impact
Even 10% of total shares can overwhelm a thinly traded small cap

body.title: Convert the Pledge
body.question: A promoter holds 40% of a company, and screener.in shows a Pledged percentage of 75%. What percentage of the company's total shares is pledged?
body.explanation: 40% × 75% = 30% of total shares. Screener.in's 75% is measured against the promoter's stake, not the whole company. Thirty percent of the entire share capital is sitting with lenders as collateral, which is a large block of potential forced selling.

body.caption: A working guide to pledge levels (as % of promoter holding)

cells: Still confirm there are no other encumbrances such as non-disposal undertakings
Low, often for personal or group liquidity
Note it and watch the trend each quarter
Meaningful; promoter depends on borrowed money
Find the stated reason, check the group's debt, and work out how far the price can fall before triggers hit
High; lenders hold effective influence over control
Treat as a major red flag unless the pledge is clearly temporary and falling

body.text: The trend beats the level. A pledge rising from 5% to 35% in four quarters, especially while the share price is falling, tells you the promoter is borrowing more against a shrinking asset. That is far more dangerous than a steady 30% pledge that has not moved in five years.

children.text: What SEBI Requires Promoters to Disclose

After a run of pledge-driven stock collapses in 2018 and 2019, SEBI tightened the rules under Regulation 31 of the SAST Regulations. Promoters must disclose every creation, invocation, or release of an encumbrance, and the definition of encumbrance was widened to include non-disposal undertakings, where the promoter promises a lender not to sell shares without formally pledging them. Pledges made through these side arrangements used to be invisible to investors.

body.text: Screener.in's Pledged percentage is based on shares formally pledged. For the full picture, open the promoter encumbrance disclosures in the company's exchange announcements on BSE or NSE, which also cover non-disposal undertakings and other encumbrances, along with the stated reason when the thresholds are crossed.

columns.label: Less Concerning
points: A small, one-time pledge to subscribe to the company's own rights issue
Short-term liquidity for a clearly disclosed personal need, with a release soon after
Pledge level stable or falling for several quarters
Released pledges repaid from dividends or other genuine income

columns.label: Red Flags
points: Funding losses or debt in unlisted group companies
Pledge rising quarter after quarter, especially as the stock falls
Repeated top-ups, visible as new pledge disclosures in quick succession
Pledge 'released' only because the lender invoked and sold the shares

body.title: Check the Mechanics
body.textWithBlank: If a promoter's loan amount stays the same and the share price falls, the loan-to-value ratio on the pledge ___.
body.explanation: LTV = Loan ÷ (Shares × Price). With the loan fixed, a lower price shrinks the denominator, so LTV rises and moves closer to the margin call and invocation triggers.

body.title: The Pledge That Keeps Growing
body.scenario: You hold a small cap listed on NSE. The promoter owns 52%. Over the last four quarters, screener.in's Pledged percentage has gone from 12% to 45%, and the stock has fallen 40% over the same period. The latest encumbrance disclosure on BSE gives the reason as 'working capital requirements of group companies'. On the concall, the MD says the pledge is 'a routine financing arrangement' and the business has never been stronger. Average daily traded volume is about 0.1% of total shares.
body.prompt: How serious is this, and what would you do? Put numbers on the risk where you can.
body.modelAnswer: This is serious. The pledge is 45% × 52% = about 23.4% of total shares, which is 234 days of average traded volume if lenders ever had to sell it, so any forced selling would crush the price. The pledge nearly quadrupled while the price fell 40%, which means the promoter has been topping up collateral against a falling stock, the classic path towards invocation. The stated reason is unlisted group companies, so the promoter is using the listed company's shares to prop up businesses you do not own and cannot see. The MD's reassurance does not match the filings. The right response is to assume the pledge is not routine, check whether the listed company has also lent to or guaranteed loans for those group companies, and seriously consider exiting before lenders are forced to, rather than waiting for the concall narrative to prove true.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Add Pledged percentage to a company's key ratios to see it at a glance, or run a screen across your holdings with a condition such as Pledged percentage > 0 to flag every stock with any promoter pledge.

body.title: Pledge Check for Your Portfolio
steps: On screener.in, create a screen or watchlist of your holdings and add Pledged percentage as a column
For any stock with a pledge, multiply promoter holding by Pledged percentage to get the pledge as a share of total shares
Compare that figure with average daily traded volume to see how many days of volume forced selling would represent
Open the promoter encumbrance disclosures in the company's BSE or NSE announcements and read the stated reason and any non-disposal undertakings
Check the last four to eight quarters: is the pledge rising, stable, or falling, and how has the share price moved alongside it?
If the pledge was released, confirm whether it was repaid or whether lenders invoked and sold the shares

points: A pledge makes promoter shares loan collateral; if the price falls far enough, the lender can invoke and sell them
LTV = Loan ÷ (Pledged Shares × Price), and Trigger Price = Current Price × Current LTV ÷ Trigger LTV
Forced selling from invoked pledges pushes prices down and triggers further margin calls, a spiral unrelated to business value
Screener.in's Pledged percentage is measured against promoter holding; multiply by promoter holding to get the share of total equity at risk
SEBI requires disclosure of every pledge event within 7 working days, and reasons once encumbrance crosses 50% of promoter holding or 20% of total shares
A rising pledge during a falling share price, funding unlisted group companies, is one of the clearest early warnings in Indian markets
